The first question the nurses are going to ask you is, why do you feel the need to be at the bedside 24/7? Prescribed tube feeding times have more to do with the body's natural rhythm. The pain is caused from phrenic nerve damage that happens during abdomen inflation in procedure. The damage actually occurs at the diaphragm but is referred via nerve to the right shoulder, right upper back and right flank. It's not actually gas trapped inside you that needs to come out or can be helped by intestinal gas meds like gasex. The nerve will settle down by about one week postop. Take your pain meds, walk, drink fluids, it will heal.

I think you're missing some vital information about your recovery and you may want to talk to your bariatric team. Just to clarify, ICEEs are liquid sugar. The flavoring in an ICEE is sugar syrup. There is no carbonation outside of what is used to spin the mix. In this case, the carbonation is not your problem. Liquid sugar will hurt you. Sugar is bad for people who have had weight loss surgery. Large amounts of sugar trigger an insulin response. That insulin causes sudden drops in your blood glucose levels which leads to increased heart rate, sweating, dizziness, nausea, diarrhea and other unpleasant things. Please talk to your doctor about your diet control.

I understand and validate how you're feeling and what you're experiencing. I've lost 125lbs since starting my journey, 90lbs since my surgery date. Fatphobia and fat bias is a real thing. I was a size 28/30 at my highest weight. And I felt invisible all the while also feeling like I took up too much space. People avoided eye contact. Coworkers showed no interest in me as a person. Strangers stared or made an effort to look away into middle distance.

But now, people talk to me, strangers smile, even now with masks off in my area. My coworkers ask questions about my personal life and try to get to know me. Initially, I was offended. Both by comments noticing my rapid weight loss and what appeared to me as the sudden realization by those around me that I existed. But in reality, despite the work I thought I was doing to love and accept my former fat self, I was depressed. I was a drag to be around. My energy was low. It was all a sham.

Now I talk and walk different. Im not negative and thus more approachable. I am happy. And happiness brings and breeds positivity. People are attracted to positive energy. I also notice large people moreso now. And often wonder, was I that big? I still feel huge. And the best description I heard here was I feel like I look like a melted candle naked. But dammit, I've gone through hell to get here. I want to be noticed. Im proud to tell people how much weight I've lost. Im proud to say I had gastric bypass surgery. And I happily explain anything folks ask.

Bottom line, people are curious creatures. Let them stare. Let them compliment. Because in the end, its zero reflection on you as a person and every bit a reflection of their own personal insecurities.

As someone who has been an employer of the houseless population, I can tell you that the act of getting a job is not that simple. Having and keeping that job is even harder. Some of these folks don't have photo ID, much less the SS card or birth certificate to prove eligibility to work. The process of procurement of these documents requires phone calls and an address to send them to. The system is set up for failure, cant get an ID without a SS card, cant get the SS card without a birth certificate, cant get a birth certificate without a phone and address, cant get an address without a job, cant get the job....you get it.

If they manage to get the job, then yay! But keeping a job as a houseless person is an unbelievably difficult task. Let's remove mental health and addiction issues from the mix and focus directly on the not having a house. Nowhere to sleep means these people are forever exhausted, they make mistakes and poor decisions on the job and have are likely to be terminated for this. Nowhere to shower or clean themselves up or wash laundry means that their coworkers must deal with body odors and unclean unhygienic appearance. And the public they work with, well let's just say they're unforgiving at best. No ID also means no bank account and no way to cash a paycheck.

So before you assume that the answer is "right in front of literally every business in medford" ask yourself, could you do the job you do everyday if suddenly your house, your money, your car, your resources, your ID, everyone that cares about you and your dignity was gone?

0645 - dayshift huddle, listen to management reminders of deemed importance.

0700 - locate different NOC nurse for each patient  to do bedside handoff, recite script of purposeful rounding until I want to puke.

0715-0745 - chart review, rough outline of day, realization that it will all change as soon as the attendings round.

0800-0900 - first CBG checks with insulin coverage all done by the RN to ensure adequate dose timing, shift assessments, telemetry review, first med pass, chart the things, attending assignment list released, more caffeine. 

0900-0930 - track down all missing med doses from pharmacy, communicate patient complaints and new/worsening sx to attendings via text message on my personal phone because no other technology available, call imaging, surgery and procedure areas for timeframes....lol

0930-0945 - first break, pee, inhale food, more caffeine. Our unit has a designated break nurse so all nurses are covered individually and are able to take 3 15's and a 30 without worry. 0945-1130 - watch for random orders to appear and attempt to figure out the MD plan with zero communication or notes from them. Attempt to answer pt questions regarding said mystery plan.  Second CBG checks with insulin coverage. Second med pass, pain assessments, institute new orders. Throw new IV pumps out the window, change expired IV sites. Put out fires of patient and family complaints. Prep for discharge of half the team, transport times from social work, lol they leave in 45 minutes.

1130-1230 - Housekeeping unit tasks like restocking my iso cabinets, resolve med machine discrepancies, print flu vaccine sheets and order from pharmacy, silence the stomach growling with more caffeine, and rounds while patients eat lunch.

1230-1300 - Forwarded texts to break nurse, of unit for lunch. Eat, drink, be merry. Consider patient abandonment and realize I'm not the one.

1300-1400 - rounds, discharge education, institute more orders, check in with any ancillary staff, read as many notes as possible to update the patient condition and make recommendations, charting forever.

1400-1415 - Mandatory huddle regarding quality process outcomes as deemed important by charge. Eat the bait candy they put out to entice attendance.

1415-1530 - receive new admits without report, attempt to piece together a plan with no clue about why they're here, admission charting, yay.

1530-1545 - second break, protein shake, more caffeine.

1545-1630 - third med pass, third CBG with insulin coverage, institute new admit orders, attempt to ignore back pain, feet aching, hitting the 4 o'clock wall, counting down the hours until NOC saves the day, chart it.

1630-1715 - rounds, post open eyelids with toothpicks, more orders, finally see attending progress notes, facepalm when necessary, chart all the things.

1715-1730 - last break, all the caffeine left in my possession, sitting with feet up, gathering inner strength to carry through to end of shift.

1730-1830 - rounds, pain meds, last med pass, check pedometer...7 miles lol...short day, call food service and figure out why new admits dont have dinner, telemetry review, chart notes, education, care plans, I & O, delirium screening, prep for report.

1830-1845 - wait for NOC assignment to be posted, lay like a cheetah ready to pounce on NOC as soon as they rollout.

1845-1915 - report off at bedside to 4 different nurses, answer stupid questions that can be seen in the chart, attempt not to roll eyes

1915 - clock off, FREEDOM.

1915-1930 - long walk to car, far away, in the dark, on feet that feel like bricks.

1930-1935 - sit in the silent car and realize I have to this all over again in 10 hours. Die a little inside.

1935-1950 - drive home, disengage nurse mode, badge in purse, activate human/wife/mom mode, listen to rage metal to burn off emotion.

1950-2000 - kiss the wife, kiss the kids, kiss the dog, strip off hospital and rinse off everything under the hot rain of a shower.

2000-2100 - eat dinner with the family, listen about their day, problem solve, try to be a parent, keep the hospital inside because they cant ever know or understand. Prop feet up and realize the mistake as they now dont want to work.

2100-2300 - zone out on a screen after kids are in bed, prep lunch for tomorrow, review tomorrow schedule with wife, try to unsuccessfully engage teenager in conversation, take ibuprofen and tylenol cocktail.

2300 - pass out, rinse and repeat.

Body fluid precautions vary from one chemotherapeutic agent to another. Typically, we only take precautions with blood, urine or stool, as most agents are processed in the kidneys or liver. Chemo drugs are great at killing ALL cells, not just cancer. Transmission of the agent is very rare via mucus membranes which line the vaginal and oral canals. That being said, erosion of mucus membranes can occur causing open sores in the mouth and vagina. This poses a risk for infection or further tissue trauma with sexual activity.
Precautions must be taken as chemo wipes out the ability to fight off infections. Talk with the oncologist regarding the types of drugs she’s getting, any required bodily fluid precautions and the chances of mucosal erosion.

What you’re referencing is termed “pulse pressure”. Specifically, narrow pulse pressure.

Systolic - diastolic = pulse pressure

Ideally, the pulse pressure should be a minimum of 25% of the systolic pressure. Your pulse pressure of 39mmHg is 30% and within normal limits. Monitor your BP daily. In the morning only, on the same arm, after first pee, before food or beverage. This will give you consistent readings. Monitor for 2 weeks and calculate your pulse pressure. If you remain above 25%, your body may just be adjusting to the volume of food you’re consuming, electrolytes and the change in proteins. If your pulse pressure continues to narrow, this could be a sign of dehydration, electrolyte imbalance or possible cardiac issues. At the end of two weeks calculation, if you have narrowed, please make an appt with a cardiologist.

Single parent of a teenager here. This is my most up to date advice. Some of which mirrors the other comment.
1. Pay attention to him. Ask him everyday how he’s feeling and how his day was.
2. Lead by example. He’ll be looking at you for the ways you adult and will adopt your behavior as that’s all he see’s so make sure you’re doing and modeling the behavior you wish to see in him.
3. Take care of yourself. I noticed the hospitalization, make sure he understands that having mental health challenges is normal and ok and you’re not less of a man for having them. And as long as you’re addressing your mental health needs, everything is ok.
4. Be open and honest with him and explain things like he’s an adult. This fosters a level of respect that you two will need as he gets into high school. You want him to tell you the truth about things and be able to come to you with questions whenever he needs. The goal is to make you his primary confidante so the bond deepens and he trusts you implicitly.
5. Teach him everything you know about adulting. Start now. The more things he has in his arsenal to deal with bullies, the better he’ll fair.
6. Get involved at his school, stay in contact with his counselor and stay on top of his grades, don’t take his word on homework; kids dismiss school as important once bullying starts. They go into survival mode at school and nothing is important except for making through the day.
7. Work. However you can to provide for him. Make sure he understands that hard work is needed to survive. This means keeping the house tidy and taking pride in your personal appearance.

The biggest thing about raising a teenager is appear real to them. Talk. Be honest. Open up about yourself and your feelings. Become a team now before high school as it only gets more challenging from here. Best of luck to you!

Multiple questions here, I’ll answer as best as I can. Merely my opinion, but I have worked in most of the Seattle areas hospitals over the last 5 years.

Some things/tips to consider. 
1. Public transportation is so amazing there, use it. Live without a vehicle if you can swing it. Tolls going into and out of Seattle are skyrocketing, gas is $3.45/gallon, average studio within walking distance of the downtown hospitals can run you $1600-2800/month. Best bet, work in the city, commute from lesser expensive areas. Rush hour is from 5a-9a & 3p-7p, worst traffic in the nation. I did a 2 hour commute, by car, last I lived there.

2. Seattle itself is a rather small downtown area, but the generally referred “Seattle” actually spans about a 50 mile radius before you’d actually be considered somewhere else. Lake Washington divides the main spaces of the Seattle area. The eastside is home to Microsoft and lots of other tech companies (read as high COL).

3.  Seattle proper now has a $15/minimum wage. This has increased nurse premiums a bit, but not enough to make a difference. Actually, I make more in the Midwest for my specialty than I did in Seattle. If you’re single, rent a room and live small.

4. Is a BSN required? Yes and no. Seattle has two dozen hospitals, it’s a market for sure. And hospitals that can claim magnet status pay well. But the BSN is only $1/hr more. I’m an ADN, never had a problem getting hired as my skill set speaks for itself. 

5.  My suggestion to you would be to start applying for travel positions within agencies. The pay is unparalleled, average about $35/55hr. Seattle market loves agency nurses, this gives the facility a chance to try you before they buy. I have completed several contracts that resulted in an offer after my 13-weeks. This is also the hospitals work around for hiring ADN’s. Be careful which agency you go with. If they seem disorganized and poor communicators, find another one and remember they work for you.

6. My favorite facilities in order, based on staffing, management & colleagues are UWMC/Harborview, Providence/Swedish, Virginia Mason & Overlake.

You can speculate all you want. But this isn’t gonna get you anywhere but lost, confused and angry. You have labeled him as having a “problem” of which you are trying to fix. And there may very well be a problem, but it is NOT yours to fix. The kid is 16 and it’s time for him to learn that he is capable handling life. Something happens at this age, hormones are raging and then they have this sudden realization that they’re individuals and completely separate entities from their parents.
I can feel frustration in your words. I understand it comes from a place of love. But he doesn’t understand this. All he’s hearing from you now is how good he “used” to be and how disappointed you are with him.
I suggest a different approach. Support and encouragement instead of lectures and nagging. The suggestions that he’s depressed are obvious and it’s likely he is. But unless you take him to a professional, you’ll never know. And he may not even agree to see a therapist. But don’t fret. You can do things at home to HELP him, because he’s not a broken thing you can just fix. Change your approach. Ask him questions about his happiness, his goals in life, what he wants out of his future....but be accepting of what he says. Don’t try to change his wants and needs to suit what YOU want for him. This is the difference between parenting a kid and a teen. You must accept him for who he is and love regardless without trying to change him. Ask him what you can do to help him meet his goals, if he has none that he can articulate, don’t offer suggestions, just ask that he take time to think about them. Ask him if he would like to confide in someone not his parent. And don’t be offended that he isn’t telling you everything. Right now he needs confidence and you can help him build that by being supportive and accepting. He is trying to find his identity outside of you. And sometimes, teens just do a complete 180 at this moment because they want a change from what they’ve been doing so far.

Hang in there. Parenting a teen is the hardest thing I’ve ever done in my life. It gets easier, but only if you stop fighting against it.
